newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: U.N. tribunal to arrest suspects without warning.
newsitem.headline: U.N. tribunal to arrest suspects without warning.

text.p: U.N. war crimes prosecutor Louise Arbour said on Monday she would move in future to arrest suspected war criminals from the former Yugoslavia without warning them first they were being sought.
Arbour, commenting on Friday's surprise arrest of a Serb suspect in the Croatian region of Eastern Slavonia, said her office planned a similar approach to future indictments.

U.N. war-crimes investigators, backed by the interim U.N. administration in the region (UNTAES), arrested the former Serb mayor of Vukovar, Slavko Dokmanovic, for alleged participation in a massacre of 260 Croats in November 1991.
It was the first time that U.N. personnel had apprehended a suspected war criminal anywhere in former Yugoslavia.

Arbour's office had earlier publicly charged three Serb officers of the Yugoslav federal army in connection with the Vukovar killings but the indictment against Dokmanovic, issued in April 1996, had remained secret until late last week.
The U.N. war crimes tribunal in The Hague has disclosed indictments against 76 suspects so far.

But it has only nine of them in its custody because local authorities in the former Yugoslavia have given only limited cooperation to the tribunal while NATO-led peacekeepers in Bosnia have refused to hunt down and arrest suspects.
Arbour said her office planned a change of strategy, keeping indictments secret in future, and thus raising the chance of arresting more of the accused.
"I'm determined to continue to use this method for as long as I believe it will be a successful strategy for providing us with the accused," she told a news conference.
Arbour denied resorting to trickery to capture Dokmanovic, stressing that a tribunal judge had issued an arrest warrant after reviewing the initial evidence against him.
"There is nothing 'tricky' about arresting people without giving them advance warning. That's the way police forces operate all over the world," she said.
The former senior Canadian judge refused to disclose precise details of the arrest so as not to jeopardise similar initiatives which may follow.

She also declined comment on whether the operation might provoke retaliation against UNTAES personnel who are supervising the return of the largely Serb enclave of Eastern Slavonia to Croatian government rule soon.
The Yugoslav government, meanwhile, has protested strongly, describing the arrest as a serious incident which could have "serious consequences for the peace process".
The Vukovar massacre occurred after local Serbs, backed by the Yugoslav army, staged an uprising prompted by Croatia's move to independence from federal Yugoslavia.
The indictment against the original three suspects said Yugoslav forces and Serb paramilitaries took 260 men from the local hospital to a remote location and killed them.
The three officers are now believed to be living in the Yugoslav republic of Serbia. Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic has disregarded international demands for their extradition.
Forensic experts from the U.N. tribunal exhumed the rural site at Ovcara, a few km (miles) south of Vukovar, in September and October of last year, recovering 200 bodies.
Arbour said Dokmanovic was mayor of Vukovar at the time of the massacre and would stand trial in The Hague for his personal participation in the beatings and killings which occurred there.
Local Serb leaders quoted by the Yugoslav news agency Tanjug insisted Dokmanovic had no part in war atrocities, saying he had "no position of authority" in November 1991.
